instantiated_cells.justification: The statute defines 'communicates directly with' to include contact in person and by telephone and by letter, facsimile, electronic mail, or other electronic means, covering oral/in-person and phone calls as well as written and electronic communications including emails.

Registration turns on expenditures/compensation and direct communications by any 'person' broadly defined, without enumerating lobbyist actor types like law firms, consultancies, think tanks, or agencies as specific categories.
Chapter 305 provides definitions for terms like 'person,' 'member of the executive branch,' and 'member of the legislative branch,' but does not define 'public entity' as such.

Coverage is subject to quantitative thresholds (minimum $200 per quarter by rule for expenditures/compensation and a time threshold of not more than 26 hours per quarter), which function as materiality tests exempting low-level activity.

The registration requirement applies to direct communications with one or more members of the legislative or executive branch to influence legislation or administrative action, and 'member of the executive branch' includes officers and employees of state agencies (including the governor as an executive officer).

Lobbying targets include 'members of the legislative branch' and 'members of the executive branch,' and those definitions expressly include officers, candidates, and employees of the legislature/committees and of state agencies or executive branch offices.

Communicating directly with members of the legislative branch and executive branch to influence legislation or administrative action triggers registration, covering both branches including executive officials.

The statute requires registration for compensated or expenditure-based efforts to communicate directly with members of either the legislative or executive branch to influence legislation or administrative action.
Both legislative and executive branch communications to influence legislation or administrative action are within the scope of activities requiring lobbyist registration.

The defined targets—members of the legislative branch and members of the executive branch—include officers and employees of legislative committees/legislature and state agencies/executive offices, encompassing senior officials and staff.

The statute expressly provides that Subsection (a)(2) does not require a member of the judicial, legislative, or executive branch of state government or an officer/employee of a political subdivision to register.

While many public officials/employees are exempt from registration, the statute authorizes the commission to require certain political subdivision officers/employees to file identifying information and sets compensation/expenditure thresholds and a time threshold for registration generally.
Registration and definitions are based on direct communication and spending/compensation thresholds, not on whether an entity has a public charter or special governmental protection.
The statute's lobbying coverage does not turn on ownership characteristics; it applies to any 'person' meeting communication and threshold criteria.

The lobbying definition/registration trigger is not based on organizational structure or revenue composition but on direct communications to influence legislation/administrative action combined with compensation/expenditure/time thresholds.
